title: Embedded T. rex Tooth Reveals Face-to-Face Attack 66 Million Years Ago
summary:
In the world of paleontology, finding direct evidence of dinosaur behavior is like striking gold. A fossil at Montana State University's Museum of the Rockies does just that: it's an Edmontosaurus skull with a tyrannosaur tooth still embedded in its face, capturing the final moments of a Cretaceous attack.

Unearthed in 2005 from the Hell Creek Formation, the skull is now the centerpiece of a study led by University of Alberta doctoral student Taia Wyenberg-Henzler and Museum of the Rockies Curator John Scannella. Their findings, published in PeerJ, reconstruct a 66-million-year-old encounter between predator and prey.

"Although bite marks on bones are relatively common, finding an embedded tooth is extremely rare," said Wyenberg-Henzler. "The great thing about an embedded tooth, particularly in a skull, is it gives you the identity of not only who was bitten but also who did the biting." By comparing the tooth to those of every known Hell Creek carnivore, the team confirmed it belonged to Tyrannosaurus rex.

CT scans at a local hospital provided a detailed look at how the tooth became trapped. The scans revealed no signs of healing, indicating the Edmontosaurus either died from the bite or was already dead. The tooth's position—lodged in the nose—suggests a face-to-face confrontation. "Looking at the way the tooth is embedded in the nose of the Edmontosaurus suggests that it met its attacker face-to-face, something that usually happens to an animal that was killed by a predator," Wyenberg-Henzler explained. The force required to break a tooth in bone implies a powerful, lethal bite.

This fossil adds a crucial data point to the long-standing debate over T. rex's hunting versus scavenging habits. While not definitive proof of active predation, the face-to-face orientation and lack of healing strongly support a predatory attack. It's a rare, visceral snapshot of life—and death—in the Age of Dinosaurs, offering a tangible connection to one of Earth's most iconic predators.
why_it_matters: Direct evidence of dinosaur behavior turns abstract monsters into real animals with daily struggles, helping students see science not as a list of facts but as a detective story that can still surprise us millions of years later.

background_read: The Hell Creek Formation, dating to the very end of the Cretaceous 66 million years ago, has yielded some of the most iconic dinosaur fossils, including T. rex and Triceratops. The area was once a humid floodplain near an inland sea that covered much of North America.

Taia Wyenberg-Henzler, the study's lead author and a PhD student at the University of Alberta, specializes in dinosaur feeding behavior. The museum curator, John Scannella, oversees the Museum of the Rockies' massive collection, which includes one of the world's largest assemblages of T. rex specimens.

Previous evidence for T. rex hunting includes healed bite marks on Edmontosaurus bones that show the prey survived, but this tooth-in-the-face scenario is far rarer because it captures the moment of the attack itself, not just its aftermath.

The K-Pg extinction event that wiped out all non-avian dinosaurs occurred around the same time as this fossil, meaning this may be one of the last predator-prey interactions before the age of dinosaurs ended.

DISCOVERY: Edmontosaurus skull found in 2005 at Hell Creek Formation
STUDY: Led by Taia Wyenberg-Henzler (U of Alberta) and John Scannella (Museum of the Rockies), published in PeerJ
IDENTITY OF BITTER: Comparison to all known Hell Creek carnivores confirms it's T. rex
FORENSIC EVIDENCE: CT scans show no healing, position in nose = face-to-face confrontation
└─ quote: 'met its attacker face-to-face, something that usually happens to an animal that was killed by a predator'

├─ ARGUMENT: Face-to-face orientation and lethal bite force support active predation
└─ CAUTION: Not definitive proof, but a crucial data point
CONCLUSION: Rare snapshot of life and death in the Age of Dinosaurs

perspectives.perspective: Positive: A thrilling piece of physical evidence that strongly supports T. rex as an active predator.
perspectives.description: For paleontologists, this is the closest we can get to witnessing a dinosaur attack. It reinforces the image of T. rex as a fearsome hunter and provides a rare behavioral window that textbooks can now illustrate with a real specimen.

perspectives.perspective: Negative / critical: A single fossil cannot settle the hunter-scavenger debate; skeptics note the dinosaur could have been already dead when bitten.
perspectives.description: Some scientists argue that even a face-to-face embedded tooth doesn't rule out scavenging if the Edmontosaurus was lying on its side. Without more examples, one fossil remains an anecdote, not a pattern.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / analytical: This fossil highlights how rare direct behavioral evidence is in paleontology, and how much interpretation depends on context.
perspectives.description: The field usually relies on trace fossils, computer models, and comparison to modern animals. A singular embedded tooth is powerful because it captures an instant, but it also reveals the limits—millions of years of missing detail can still cloud the full picture.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking: Future CT technology and more Hell Creek discoveries could build a stronger case.
perspectives.description: As scanning tools improve and more fossils are carefully excavated, paleontologists hope to find similar 'frozen moments' that can statistically show whether such face-to-face attacks were common, painting a clearer picture of predator-prey dynamics right before the dinosaurs vanished.
